title: AI Is All Over This Year's Political Ads: How to Spot a Fake Before You Share It
summary: Over $137 million has been spent on AI-generated political ads this cycle, and most carry no disclosure. Here is a practical checklist for spotting fakes before you share.
before: Political ads show real footage. If something looks off, you will notice it immediately.
after: AI-generated ads are everywhere, most have no label, and the fakes are getting harder to spot.
body:
This election cycle, AI-generated political ads have gone from curiosity to mainstream. The technology is cheap, fast, and increasingly convincing. If you have seen a political ad in the last few months, there is a good chance part of it was made by software. Here is what you need to know to navigate this new reality without getting fooled.

## The Numbers Are Staggering

According to the Wesleyan Media Project, campaigns and political groups have spent more than **$137 million** on AI-generated or AI-enhanced ads ahead of the 2026 midterms. That is a massive jump from the 2024 cycle, when the same researchers identified less than $50,000 in AI ad spending.

The project has tracked over 220 unique AI-generated ads across 34 states. But here is the uncomfortable part: only about **27% of those ads included any disclosure** that AI was involved. The remaining 70% or so carried no label at all.

For voters, this creates a campaign environment where an ad can look like conventional political video even when what appears on screen was generated or altered by software.

## What These Ads Actually Look Like

AI political ads range from subtle enhancements to outright fabrications. Some use AI to clean up audio or generate stock-style background imagery. Others are more brazen.

One example that drew national attention: Republican New York gubernatorial candidate Bruce Blakeman released an AI-generated ad showing Governor Kathy Hochul and New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani in a mock drug commercial for "delusion pills." The ad depicted the two politicians bizarrely gardening together and riding bikes in scenes that never happened. It carried no AI disclaimer. State Democrats filed a Board of Elections complaint, arguing the ad violated New York's law requiring "materially deceptive" content to be labeled.

This is not an isolated case. Researchers at Wesleyan found that nearly half of the AI ads they tracked showed AI-generated versions of real politicians doing or saying things that never occurred.

## The Regulation Patchwork

There is no federal law requiring disclosure of AI in political ads. Efforts in Congress and at the Federal Election Commission have stalled.

Into that vacuum, states have stepped in. As of October 2026, 30 states have enacted some form of law regulating AI-generated media in political advertising. Most require disclosures, while a handful (Maryland, Minnesota, Texas) prohibit certain election deepfakes outright, even with a disclaimer.

But state laws vary widely in scope and enforcement, and many ads identified by researchers ran without disclosure even in states with laws on the books. AI-generated ads that can be interpreted as satire or parody are often exempt from disclosure requirements, which creates obvious loopholes.

## A Simple Checklist for Spotting Fakes

Visual detection is harder than you might think. Studies show people often overestimate their ability to identify deepfakes. But there are practical steps you can take:

- **Check the source first.** Before analyzing pixels, ask: Where did this video come from? Is it from an official campaign account, a verified news outlet, or a random social media post? This question matters more than any visual tell.
- **Watch for lip-sync issues.** Replay a short section at slower speed. Do the lips form the sounds you hear? Mismatched lip movements remain one of the most reliable combined tells.
- **Look at edges and hands.** AI models still struggle with hands (extra fingers, fused digits) and with the boundary between a face and its background. Hairlines, jaw edges, and shadows near the collar can expose a weak composite.
- **Check blinking and expressions.** Inconsistent blink cadence and expressions that do not quite match the emotional context can be flags, though top-tier AI is closing this gap.
- **Run a reverse image or video search.** Tools like Google Lens or TinEye can help locate the original source and determine whether content was manipulated.

Important caveat: no single visual glitch proves a video is fake. These cues are supporting evidence, not definitive proof. The best approach combines visual inspection with source verification.

## The Mindset That Matters Most

**Pause before you share.** This is the single most important habit you can adopt. Deepfakes thrive on speed and emotion. If a video makes you angry, outraged, or triumphant, that is exactly when you should slow down.

Ask yourself: Have I verified this with a separate, trusted source? Is this claim being reported by credible news outlets? If the answer is no or not yet, wait.

The goal is not to become a forensic video analyst. The goal is to add a few seconds of friction between seeing something and amplifying it. In an environment where most AI ads carry no disclosure and detection is imperfect, that small pause is your best defense.
